enrichment.short_title: Bidoon asylum appeal remitted for inadequate IAT reasons
key_facts: A Kuwaiti Bidoon failed asylum seeker appealed after the Immigration Appeal Tribunal allowed his appeal on returnability and human rights grounds.
The IAT found inter-governmental negotiations for return would inevitably disclose his asylum claim, breaching confidentiality assurances.
The Court of Appeal held the disclosure finding was unsupported by evidence and the Secretary of State had no opportunity to respond.
The tribunal failed to identify why this appellant, as opposed to Bidoon generally, faced persecution or Article 3 ill-treatment on return.
The tribunal's expression of doubt was treated as reversing the well-founded fear burden of proof under Sivakumaran.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State's appeal to the Court of Appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision allowing a limited asylum and human rights appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; IAT decision quashed and case remitted to a differently constituted tribunal for fresh consideration.
enrichment.ratio: An immigration tribunal must identify case-specific reasons why an individual qualifies for protection rather than resting on general group disadvantage; findings on disclosure and confidentiality must be evidence-based and procedurally fair, and doubt about persecution cannot substitute for applying the Sivakumaran test that a reasonable likelihood of Convention-related persecution must be demonstrated.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred in finding return negotiations would inevitably disclose the asylum claim
Whether breach of interview confidentiality could support allowing the appeal
Whether the tribunal identified individualised persecution or Article 3 risk for the appellant
Whether the tribunal reversed the burden of proof on well-founded fear of persecution

enrichment.short_title: Parole release veto for 15-year-plus prisoners upheld
key_facts: Mr Clift was serving 18 years for attempted murder and GBH with intent and became eligible for parole in March 2002.
The Parole Board recommended release but the Home Secretary refused, citing recent behavioural improvement, missing offence-related work, and an unsupportive psychologist's report.
The claimant challenged the refusal as irrational and argued that retaining Home Secretary release power for prisoners serving 15 years or more breached Article 5 read with Article 14.
Under the 1998 Order, prisoners serving less than 15 years are released by the Parole Board alone; those serving 15 years or more require Home Secretary approval after a Board recommendation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's decision refusing parole release following a positive Parole Board recommendation.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Article 14 challenge rejected and permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Different parole decision-makers for prisoners serving just under and just over 15 years engage Article 14 within the ambit of Article 5, but reserving final release decisions on long determinate sentences to the Home Secretary pursues the legitimate aim of public safety and is proportionate despite some arbitrariness at the cut-off.
legal_issues: Whether the Home Secretary's refusal of parole was irrational
Whether Article 5 taken with Article 14 is engaged by differential parole release procedures
Who are the appropriate comparators for prisoners near the 15-year threshold
Whether the 15-year cut-off is objectively justified

enrichment.short_title: Construction adjudicator decision unenforceable after undisclosed expert report

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Scheme for Construction Contracts (England and Wales) Regulations 1998

key_facts: RSL sought summary judgment to enforce an adjudicator's decision awarding about £93,204 on a DOM/2 sub-contract final account dispute.
The adjudicator employed a planning consultant, Mr Adie, with parties' consent subject to Stansell's conditions including sight of reports and time to comment.
Stansell received and could comment on Mr Adie's preliminary report but not his final report, which materially informed the extension-of-time decision.
The judge held enforcement would breach natural justice because decisive material was not disclosed and Stansell's conditional consent created a legitimate expectation of comment.
An alternative interim payment or severance of unaffected parts of the decision was rejected as conceptually incompatible with contractual adjudication enforcement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for summary judgment or interim payment to enforce a construction adjudicator's decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; adjudicator's decision held unenforceable for breach of natural justice and action dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator must afford both parties an opportunity to comment on any material, including an expert's final report, that the adjudicator intends to rely on; where consent to employ an expert is given on terms requiring disclosure and comment, failure to provide that opportunity renders the decision unenforceable even in the speedy adjudication context.
legal_issues: Whether Stansell's consent to employ Mr Adie was conditional on disclosure and comment rights
Whether natural justice required comment on the final expert report
Whether the adjudicator wrongfully delegated the extension-of-time decision
Whether an enforceable part of the adjudicator's decision could be severed or recovered by interim payment

enrichment.short_title: Football chant using 'Paki' held racialist under 1991 Act
key_facts: Sean Ratcliffe admitted joining Port Vale supporters chanting 'you're just a town full of Pakis' at a designated match against Oldham Athletic.
The chant was audible to opposing supporters; no Asian or black persons were present in the crowd or on the pitch.
The district judge acquitted on submission that the words were mere doggerel and 'Paki' was no more insulting than 'Aussie' or 'Brit'.
The DPP appealed by case stated asking whether the evidence entitled acquittal on the ground the chanting was not of a racialist nature.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated by the Director of Public Prosecutions against magistrates' acquittal at the close of the prosecution case.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted with direction to convict on the admitted evidence.
enrichment.ratio: The word 'Paki' in modern usage is racially offensive slang, and in the context of a football chant directed at supporters of another town it is insulting by reason of nationality or ethnic origin within section 3(2)(b); presence or offence taken by members of the racial group referred to is immaterial.
legal_issues: Meaning of chanting 'of a racialist nature' under section 3(2)(b)
Whether 'Paki' is insulting by reason of nationality or ethnic origin
Whether context and absence of targeted persons defeat the offence
Proper approach to dictionary and sentencing authority on racial abuse

enrichment.short_title: Fly-posting prosecution and reverse burden under section 224

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Control of Advertisements) Regulations 1992

key_facts: Christodoulou, a director of Secrets Night Club, was prosecuted for 14 fly-posting offences advertising events in Barking and Dagenham.
Enforcement officers photographed numerous posters miles from Romford; the club claimed promoters, not the director, were responsible.
Magistrates held there was no case to answer because knowledge or consent of display had not been proved.
Section 224(4)(b) deems a person to display an advertisement giving publicity to his trade or business; section 224(5)(b) provides a defence if display was without knowledge or consent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated by the local planning authority against magistrates' no-case-to-answer ruling.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to magistrates for rehearing by a fresh bench; no order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where advertisements publicise a defendant's business he is deemed to display them under section 224(4)(b) and the prosecution need not prove knowledge or consent; the reverse evidential burden under section 224(5)(b) means magistrates erred in treating absence of proof of knowledge as fatal at the close of the prosecution case.
legal_issues: Construction of section 224(4) deeming provision for fly-posting
Whether prosecution must prove knowledge or consent before conviction
Effect of promoter invoices and club policy prohibiting fly-posting
Article 6 compatibility of the reverse burden of proof

enrichment.short_title: Unlawful immigration detention after successful asylum appeal
key_facts: A Somali national was detained under Schedule 3 after serving a three-year sentence for indecent assault and a deportation order.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal allowed his appeal on 29 November 2002, finding refugee status and Article 3 risk on return to Somalia.
The Secretary of State continued detention while considering a late and weak appeal application and then an out-of-time Court of Appeal application raising Article 33(2).
The claimant was released on 10 April 2003; Kay J found detention unlawful from about 21 December 2002 for lack of careful reappraisal under Hardial Singh principles.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review challenging lawfulness of immigration detention pending deportation after a successful IAT asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; declaration that detention from 21 December 2002 to 10 April 2003 was unlawful; damages claim adjourned.
enrichment.ratio: Detention under Schedule 3 paragraph 2(3) is authorised only for a period reasonably necessary pending removal; once removal is not realistically imminent and appeal prospects are weak, continued detention after a successful tribunal decision requires careful reappraisal and otherwise becomes unlawful under Hardial Singh.
legal_issues: Whether detention remained 'pending removal' after the IAT allowed the asylum appeal
Application of Hardial Singh limits on deportation detention
Relevance of absconding risk and further offending to reasonableness of detention length
Lawfulness of continued detention after expiry of time for an in-time Court of Appeal application

enrichment.short_title: Ten-year enforcement limit focused on particular breach in notice
key_facts: A 1964 planning permission required the whole basement car park to be retained for occupiers and users of the Clarges Street building.
Fourteen of nineteen spaces had been used by outsiders for over ten years and were immune from enforcement; five spaces were still enforced against.
The appellant argued the condition was breached as a whole more than ten years ago, so all enforcement was time-barred under section 171B(3).
The inspector upheld enforcement for the five spaces; Sullivan J dismissed the section 289 appeal on a different but related construction of the ten-year limit.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 289 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 against a planning inspector's dismissal of enforcement notice appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; enforcement notices for the five remaining spaces upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Section 171B(3) must be read with sections 172 to 174 so the ten-year bar applies to the particular matters alleged in the enforcement notice and the remedial steps required, not merely to any historical breach of the condition as a whole; immunity for one part of a site does not extinguish enforcement rights in respect of a separately identified continuing breach.
legal_issues: Whether breach of a condition requiring retention of the whole car park became immune after ten years
Construction of 'the whole of the car-parking accommodation' in condition 2
Whether enforcement can target individual spaces after partial immunity
Interaction between section 171B and enforcement notice particulars under section 173

enrichment.short_title: Article 8 certification upheld for Dublin return to Germany
key_facts: A Turkish asylum seeker with prior asylum claims in Germany married a British citizen after third-country removal directions were set.
The Secretary of State certified his Article 8 allegation as manifestly unfounded under section 72(2), removing appeal rights while in the UK.
The appellant argued removal to Germany would fail the entry clearance rules because his wife would have increased recourse to public funds.
The Court of Appeal held whether he would qualify for entry clearance is for the entry clearance officer later, not at certification stage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of judicial review of the Secretary of State's section 72(2)(a) certification that an Article 8 claim was manifestly unfounded.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; certification and proposed return to Germany upheld as proportionate.
enrichment.ratio: Temporary separation to require a third-country asylum seeker to apply overseas for spouse entry clearance is not manifestly unfounded under section 72(2)(a) merely because entry clearance might ultimately be refused; eligibility for clearance is determined on application, and Article 8 can be weighed at that stage including any discretion outside the rules.
legal_issues: Whether return to Germany pending entry clearance application breaches Article 8
Proper approach to section 72(2)(a) manifestly unfounded certification after Thangarasa
Whether inability to meet Rule 281(v) without recourse to public funds defeats certification
Relevance of marriage formed while subject to removal directions

enrichment.short_title: Law Society jurisdiction over post-retainer solicitor conduct
key_facts: Mr Haycocks settled a client complaint with Law Society approval in September 2000, agreeing to return files and French property deeds.
He breached the agreement by failing to return files and belatedly returning deeds; the Office for the Supervision of Solicitors reopened the complaint.
An adjudicator found substandard services proved and awarded the £5,000 maximum compensation for anxiety and distress.
The Court of Appeal held Schedule 1A jurisdiction covers professional services connected with matters in which the solicitor was instructed, including post-retainer agreement compliance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of permission for judicial review of OSS compensation decision, treated as proceeding in the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.outcome: No order on judicial review application; Law Society undertook to reconsider compensation quantum in light of corrected facts.
enrichment.ratio: Schedule 1A of the Solicitors Act 1974 empowers the Law Society to act where professional services in connection with a matter in which the solicitor was instructed have not been of reasonable quality, including failure to honour a complaint settlement agreement to return client documents after retainer termination.
legal_issues: Whether OSS had jurisdiction over conduct after termination of retainer
Whether a complaint settlement agreement is a matter in which the solicitor was instructed
Whether maximum compensation under Schedule 1A was irrational or based on factual error
Overlap between quality of service and professional misconduct
catchwords: Office for the Supervision of Solicitors

confidence.notes: Clear jurisdiction ruling; compensation remitted by agreement so final quantum not decided by the court.

enrichment.short_title: Contact orders reinstated with facilitative family expert
key_facts: A father sought contact with two teenage daughters aged 14 and nearly 16 after protracted litigation and alleged parental alienation.
CAFCASS Legal had been appointed guardian following an earlier Court of Appeal judgment in February 2002, but progress stalled until late 2002.
Contact orders were terminated in November and December 2002 without satisfactory process; the girls had expressed reluctance to engage but remained in informal contact with their father.

The President reinstated contact applications adjourned generally and directed CAFCASS Legal to instruct a mental health expert in a facilitative mediation mode rather than for further contested litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal granted and treated as the appeal against termination of contact orders in private law Children Act proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed to limited extent; father's contact applications reinstated and adjourned generally; expert facilitation ordered; no order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where teenage children's welfare would benefit from rebuilding a relationship with a parent, the court may reinstate adjourned contact applications and direct facilitative expert intervention to avoid further orders, especially as section 9(6) makes contact orders exceptional after age 16 and section 1(5) requires that an order be better for the child than no order.
legal_issues: Whether termination of contact orders in November 2002 was procedurally satisfactory
Appropriate role of CAFCASS Legal and mental health experts in intractable contact disputes
Whether court orders remain appropriate for children approaching 16
Facilitative versus adjudicative use of expert evidence in family proceedings
